items.t: VSAT, AVAV, LMT Secure Multi-Million-Dollar Defense Contracts This Week — But One Stock Stole The Spotlight
sum: Despite concerns that Democrats’ midterm election sweep could cloud the outlook for defense spending, defense contractors, including Lockheed Martin (LMT), Viasat (VSAT) and AeroVironment (AVAV), secured multimillion-dollar military contracts this week.
However, the biggest gainer this week was AEVEX (AVEX), which signed a roughly $400-million drone contract.

AeroVironment announced a $405-million international order for its LOCUST X3 laser-defense systems, designed to destroy enemy drones using directed high-energy laser systems. The company highlighted Shahed-series one-way attack drones, which have been frequently used in the ongoing U.S.-Israel-Iran war, as a potential target.

Separately, AeroVironment also secured an initial $315 million U.S. government award under a multiyear contract with a potential value of $940 million. It did not identify the customer or program, citing operational security restrictions.

Viasat won a $450-million U.S. Space Force contract to develop secure satellite communications infrastructure supporting military operations and the Golden Dome missile-defense initiative. The agreement includes an initial $115 million task order.
Meanwhile, AEVEX (AVEX) announced a multi-year drone contract with a potential value approaching $400 million for unmanned aircraft systems and support services.
On Tuesday, Ondas (ONDS) received an additional military drone order under its Digital Bat program, although financial terms were not disclosed.

Lockheed Martin stock reaches 100,000th GMLRS delivery milestone
sum: Lockheed Martin announced on Tuesday, November 10, that it had delivered its 100,000th Guided Multiple Launch Rocket System rocket and reached an annual production rate of nearly 14,000 units ahead of schedule. The company disclosed the milestones at its Camden, Arkansas, facility in a Lockheed Martin press release.

Lockheed Martin said the production pace reflects rising demand for a combat-proven precision weapon used by the U.S. Army and allied forces. GMLRS rockets are launched from M270 and HIMARS systems, giving the program a direct role in replenishing and expanding precision-fire inventories.

The company also reported that it and General Dynamics Ordnance and Tactical Systems had completed the first test of a new solid rocket motor for GMLRS. Further testing is planned, with qualification targeted for 2027. If successful, the effort would establish a third domestic source for a key component and reduce dependence on a narrower supplier base.

Lockheed Martin vice president Gaylia Campbell said the company was investing in suppliers and coordinating with the Department of War and industry partners to meet demand. General Dynamics executive Chris Haynes described the motor test as a milestone in expanding domestic solid rocket motor capacity. Neither company disclosed test results or the additional annual output that a qualified motor line could support.

The GMLRS program includes more than 200 suppliers across 35 states, with more than 50 designated as small businesses. More than 200 employees support GMLRS production at Camden, while Lockheed Martin is hiring 50% more workers at the site for accelerated output across GMLRS, PAC-3 MSE and the Precision Strike Missile.

The expansion broadens Camden's role beyond a single missile line and links the GMLRS milestone to a wider U.S. effort to build domestic munitions capacity. For investors, the key execution question is whether the new motor can progress from initial testing to qualification in 2027 while the company sustains the higher production rate.

What Could Lockheed Martin Stock Be Worth In Three Years?
sum: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

Lockheed Martin (LMT) stock returned 35.0% over the past year, compared to 13.1% for the S&P 500. Anyone buying now is betting the company keeps selling more. Management raised its sales outlook for 2026 again in October, and Lockheed ended September with a record order backlog. So how much is left for someone buying at today’s $603.12?
Under the scenario set out below, a Lockheed Martin share would be worth about $794.86 three years from now, or 31.8% more than today’s price. That works out to 9.6% a year, before dividends.

This scenario grows revenue by 9.8% a year, a quarter faster than the 7.9% Lockheed reported over the twelve months to September 2026. Trefis holds the P/E at today’s level. It then blends today’s net margin, at a 70% weight, with its average at earlier quarter ends. The table sets today’s figures beside those three years out.

All of the gain therefore comes from higher revenue, with nothing added from a richer margin or P/E. Third-quarter sales rose 11% to $20.7 billion. Management said higher volume across every segment was behind the increase, including F-35 production at Aeronautics and munitions production at Missiles and Fire Control.

Management expects all four of Lockheed’s segments to grow sales in 2027. The company ended September with a backlog of $292 billion, up $113 billion from a year earlier. That figure represents about 3.7 times what Lockheed sold over the latest twelve months.

The largest addition in the third quarter was a seven-year PAC-3 missile contract, now worth up to $58.6 billion in total, management said. Management expects sales at Missiles and Fire Control to grow in the mid-teens a year on average over the next five years. A new F-35 agreement also sets a path to 850 U.S. aircraft over ten years, management said. For the whole company, management sees high single-digit revenue growth in 2027, which may be slower than the scenario’s pace; its raised 2026 sales outlook of $80 billion to $82 billion adds little, since three quarters of that year are already in the trailing figures.

Why Lockheed Martin Rallied in October
sum: Shares of Lockheed Martin (NYSE:LMT) rallied 25.1% in October, according to data from S&P Global Market Intelligence.

The largest defense contractor rallied on the back of strong third-quarter earnings last month. On top of the strong results, the company closed longer-term deals with the Department of Defense, earning increased confidence from the analyst community.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »
Lockheed beats expectations as missiles and aircraft rule the day

In the third quarter, Lockheed saw its revenue rise 11.3% to $20.7 billion, while diluted earnings per share grew 14.6% to $7.95. Both figures handily beat analyst expectations. Management also raised its full-year guidance to a revenue range of $80 billion to $82 billion, up by $250 million on both ends, and diluted EPS to a range of $30.35 to $30.75, up from $29.95 to $30.65 previously.

Lockheed benefited from strong growth in its Aeronautics division, which produces the F-35 fighter jet, and Missiles and Fire Control, which is seeing outsize growth due to missile use in the war in Iran and the Russia-Ukraine conflict. Aeronautics rallied 13.2%, while Missiles and Fire Control grew 24.2%.

Management also announced that the Department of Defense had finalized a 10-year agreement for F-35s, with a minimum of 850 aircraft to be sold over the period, and Lockheed guaranteeing a production capacity of 156 aircraft per year. Guaranteeing a sales floor will enable Lockheed to fund the expansion itself, which should, in theory, reduce or delay government outlays. Lockheed also signed another agreement with the Department of Defense to accelerate production of the Joint Advanced Tactical Missile.

How much SpaceX stock does CEO Elon Musk actually own?
sum: After Space Exploration Technologies, or SpaceX for short, went public in June 2026, Elon Musk's financial status vaulted from multibillionaire to trillionaire — the world's first trillionaire ever.

Musk founded SpaceX in 2002, and the company was initially widely dismissed for moving into an aerospace industry already dominated by defense contractors such as Boeing and Lockheed Martin. Over the years, SpaceX's successes included landing a contract with NASA in 2008 and leading innovation in the field with vertical landings of its rocket boosters in 2015. Now, Musk has his eyes set on space exploration and human colonization of Mars.
Here's a closer look at how many shares Musk owns in SpaceX, what his stake is worth, and how he accumulated so much stock in the company.

Elon Musk owned 6.4 billion shares, equating to about 48.4% of the company, according to an August 2026 filing with the SEC. Those shares — which came from both Class A and Class B common stock — were valued at $872 billion, as of early November 2026.
Of Musk's SpaceX holdings, at least 3.9 billion are Class B super-voting shares. These shares carry 10 times the voting power of ordinary shares, giving Musk over 80% of the company's voting power.
Still, of the 6.4 billion shares, there were 1.3 billion shares of restricted Class B common stock.
Elon Musk is the largest individual shareholder of SpaceX, and he controls almost half of the company's outstanding shares. Institutional investors are the next biggest holders of SpaceX stock.

NASA shares major Moon Base updates at the MAX POWER expo: Here’s what comes next
sum: NASA shares Moon Base updates at the MAX POWER expo, including a nuclear-powered rover and new lander deals

A permanent lunar base will need much more than just astronauts. It will need reliable supply transport, power systems, scouting vehicles, and much more. And to turn this ambitious vision into reality, NASA has announced major updates to its contracts and lunar landers that will fill gaps in its Moon Base program. The details were shared during the agency’s two-day MAX POWER aerospace expo, which is currently being held at the Kennedy Space Center in Florida and will run till November 08, 2026.

More momentum for the Moon Base! NASA has awarded six new launch and in-space transportation task orders to American companies, advancing the capabilities for future missions supporting Moon Base such as CAPSTONE 02, LCRNS, and MoonFall.

As part of its latest update, NASA selected eight companies for the next stage of its Commercial Lunar Payload Services program, known as CLPS. These are the companies that will help build and take payloads from Earth to the surface of the Moon. With this, the first elements of the Moon Base will already be on the surface when astronauts return with Artemis IV. According to the announcement, the selected group is Blue Origin, Firefly Aerospace, Intuitive Machines, iSpace US, Lockheed Martin Space, Northrop Grumman Space Systems, SpaceX, and Voyager Technologies.

Voyager has been selected for @NASA CLPS 2 contract, making it eligible to compete for future lunar missions through 2036 under a $10 billion base ceiling. The selection expands its role in the Moon Base Program as Griffin-1 prepares for launch to the lunar South Pole. Learn more at https://t.co/POij0YHyii. $VOYG #AcceleratingtheAdvantage #MissionReady

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said, “We are building the Moon Base mission by mission. Today’s announcements expand nearly every part of that campaign, using the playbook that carried NASA through its greatest eras: fly often, learn, apply those lessons, and get more better and more capable with every mission. When our astronauts return to the Moon, they will arrive with the first elements of the Moon Base already waiting for them on the surface.”

Lockheed Martin's (NYSE: LMT) Record $292 Billion Backlog And Valuation Discount Make A Compelling Investment Case
sum: A book-to-bill ratio of 4.0 in the third quarter of 2026 signals that Lockheed Martin (NYSE: LMT) is pulling in new orders at a pace that far outstrips its current revenue base.
That demand surge pushed the company’s backlog to a record $292 billion as of September 27, 2026, up sharply from $230 billion just one quarter earlier.
Despite that extraordinary momentum, LMT shares trade at a forward 12-month price-to-sales ratio of just 1.56X, a meaningful discount to the aerospace-defense industry average of 2.16X.
That valuation gap has emerged even as the stock has climbed 12% over the past six months, a period during which the broader Zacks Aerospace-Defense industry fell 8.8%.

The outperformance reflects a wave of major contract awards, including a seven-year PAC-3 missile defense agreement valued at up to $58.6 billion and a separate seven-year THAAD deal worth $35 billion.

Allied demand for advanced air and missile defense systems also drove a $439 million ATACMS production contract tied to Taiwan’s HIMARS launchers and an $800 million award for Australia’s AIR6500 battle management program.
On October 26, 2026, Lockheed completed its $3.45 billion acquisition of Ultra Maritime, a specialist in undersea and anti-submarine warfare technologies serving allied naval forces globally.

Is Lockheed Martin Stock Priced Right Against Its Peers?
sum: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

Lockheed Martin (LMT) keeps more of its sales as operating profit than four of its five aerospace and defense peers, tying the fifth, RTX. The stock returned 25.1% from November 3, 2025 to November 4, 2026, the best in the group. Yet on price against earnings, Lockheed ranks only fourth of the five companies with a usable P/E. If not the margin, what are investors paying for in this group?

Investors in this group appear to pay for sales growth more than for margin. On growth, Lockheed also ranks fourth of six companies. RTX shows the contrast most sharply. Over their latest four quarters, both companies kept 11.8% of sales as operating profit, yet investors pay 31.9 times earnings for RTX against 21.1 for Lockheed. One difference between the two is sales growth: RTX grew revenue 11.6% over that period, against 7.9% for Lockheed.

Most of the rest of the group fits the same pattern. General Dynamics grows faster than Lockheed and trades at a slightly higher P/E, while Northrop Grumman grows slower and trades lower. Only L3Harris is priced above Lockheed with slower growth.

In 2025, Lockheed's missiles business, Missiles and Fire Control, grew sales 13.6% to $15.3 billion. Its largest business, Aeronautics, which makes the F-35 jet, grew more slowly, up 5.7% to $30.6 billion.

Lockheed's growth over the past four quarters includes a first quarter of fiscal 2026 in which sales barely rose from a year earlier. Sales then grew 10.5% in the second quarter and 11.3% in the third. Management said every segment grew in the third quarter, and sales at Missiles and Fire Control rose 24%.

Lockheed also ended the third quarter with a record $292 billion backlog, the orders it has yet to turn into sales. That is up $113 billion from a year earlier. The largest addition in the quarter was a seven-year contract for PAC-3 interceptors.

Defense Stocks Fall After Democrats Win Congress, Putting 2027 Budget in Focus
sum: Defense stocks fell Wednesday after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress, as investors assessed whether the new majority would challenge President Donald Trump’s defense spending priorities.

Lockheed Martin shares fell 3.6% in Wednesday’s session. L3Harris lost more than 2%, while RTX Corporation and Northrop Grumman each dropped more than 3%. The moves followed Tuesday’s midterm results and drew attention to federal budget choices that shape demand for defense contractors’ products and services.

Each company has significant government exposure. About 70% of Lockheed Martin’s sales come from the U.S. government, while U.S. government sales made up 75% of L3Harris’ fiscal 2025 revenue. L3Harris’ figure includes sales through prime contractors, including foreign military sales. RTX and Northrop Grumman also generate significant sales through U.S. government contracts.

That reliance leaves the companies exposed to congressional review of the administration’s spending agenda. Wednesday’s market reaction reflected concern that a Democratic majority could challenge President Trump’s priorities, adding uncertainty for contractors that depend on public funding.

Wolfe Research analyst Myles Walton called the Democratic sweep a “headline negative” for defense shares, but said the first reaction could be “potentially short-lived.” Walton pointed to the 2006 midterms, when Republicans held the White House and Democrats captured both chambers of Congress.

Defense shares initially fell about 2% after that election, then recovered while military budgets continued rising. Democrats later backed increased funding for U.S. operations in Iraq. The episode shows why an election result alone does not settle the direction of defense spending.

The historical comparison comes as the current backdrop includes the Iran war and the Russia-Ukraine war. A roughly 20% decline from the sector’s summer peak had already put aerospace and defense shares under pressure, a pullback discussed in an earlier analysis of a possible tactical bottom for the sector.

AI data center stocks dip, renewables surge after Democrat sweep in US midterm elections
sum: Nov 4 (Reuters) – Data center stocks slipped in premarket trading on Wednesday, while clean-energy shares surged after Democrats won both the Senate and the House, raising prospects of tougher oversight of the AI boom alongside fresh backing for renewables.
The Democrats scored sweeping victories in Republican strongholds such as Kansas for the first time in generations.
Texas and Georgia, which are key states for data centers given their ability to host large-scale facilities, also elected Democratic candidates.
The results will usher in a divided government in Washington, following two years in which the Republican-controlled Congress rarely exercised its power to rein in President Donald Trump.
Market reaction spanned sectors including AI-linked stocks, renewables, healthcare companies and prison operators.
Data center operators lost ground, with Core Scientific down 2.8% and Iren down 1.4%. Applied Digital and CoreWeave were marginally lower.

The data center boom triggered public backlash this year, stoking concerns that tighter Democratic oversight could curb spending momentum at a time when investors are becoming wary of mounting AI outlays yet to deliver strong financial returns.

Defense Stock Showdown: SpaceX vs. Lockheed Martin -- Which Is the Smarter Long-Term Buy?
sum: There's far more to warfare than guns and missiles. So, when thinking about defense stocks, it's important to look at every angle. On one side are traditional defense contractors, such as Lockheed Martin (LMT -1.58%), which develops and sells various weapons systems, vehicles, and other technologies to the United States government and its allies.

On the other side is Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +8.62%), or SpaceX for short. SpaceX doesn't sell weapons, but artificial intelligence (AI) and rocket launches are paramount to defending the United States moving forward. The federal government accounted for approximately a fifth of SpaceX's total revenue in 2025.
It's hard not to like SpaceX's advantages in space and AI, arguably the greatest opportunities ahead for the defense industry. But which stock is the smarter long-term buy right now?

Space offers several growth opportunities for defense companies, including satellite constellations for communications and surveillance, orbital data centers, and the Golden Dome, a planned multilayered missile defense system featuring thousands of satellites equipped with sensors and interceptors.

SpaceX offers an infrastructure angle on space and AI. It's the world's de facto leader in rocket launch services and provides global connectivity through Starlink. It would likely remain quite busy as the government continues to expand its satellite constellations. According to SpaceX, AI is its greatest opportunity, and there's government traction there, too. Court documents recently revealed that the U.S. military utilized AI technology from SpaceX's xAI to aid in Operation Epic Fury in Iran.

Lockheed Martin also has a long history with the government, including several anti-missile munitions and systems, such as NGI and THAAD interceptors, PAC-3 air defense missiles, and the SBIRS critical missile-warning system. Investors will likely find the company's software, munitions, and sensors throughout the Golden Dome.

Elon Musk is one of the greatest modern entrepreneurs, so it shouldn't come as a surprise that SpaceX is figuratively reaching for the stars. While preparing for its IPO, SpaceX estimated its total addressable market across space, connectivity, and AI at $28.5 trillion, though AI accounted for $26.5 trillion of that.

Iran Peace Deal: What Does It Mean for Defense Stocks Like Lockheed Martin?
sum: The general assumption is that a peace deal between the United States and Iran will hurt defense stocks. But it's not that simple. In fact, it's not really about whether the fighting stops now. It's about whether governments will continue spending on defense over the next decade.

Lockheed Martin (LMT -1.58%) has long benefited from demand for defense systems during peacetime and wartime. Over the past 40 years, shares of Lockheed Martin have climbed 2,500%. And while there hasn't been a complete lack of military conflict over the last four decades, the military demands have varied. Yet that has never changed the long-term trajectory of the stock.

In 2025, the company ended the year with a record backlog of approximately $194 billion, giving it years of contracted work already in hand. Lockheed also generated $75 billion in revenue during 2025, up about 6% from the prior year. Management expects sales to climb to between $77.5 billion and $80 billion in 2026.

That is not trivial, and an end to the war with Iran won't suddenly erase existing orders for fighter jets, missile-defense systems, helicopters, satellites, and other military hardware. In fact, many of Lockheed's most important programs don't rely on any single conflict.

Take the F-35, for example, which remains the backbone of air forces around the world. Lockheed delivered a record 191 F-35 aircraft in 2025, and the company still has hundreds of aircraft remaining in its production backlog.

Meanwhile, recent events in the Middle East have highlighted the importance of missile defense, as Iran's extensive use of ballistic missiles has reinforced demand for systems such as THAAD (Terminal High Altitude Area Defense) anti-ballistic missile defense system and Patriot interceptors.

In January, Lockheed signed an agreement with the Pentagon that could increase THAAD interceptor production capacity from 96 missiles annually to as many as 400. That's not an insignificant increase. And that's why you should not assume that peace automatically translates into lower defense spending.

Led by the Falcon rocket and Falcon Heavy for bigger payloads, SpaceX claimed more than 80% of global rocket launches last year and has more than 10,000 Starlink satellites in orbit. But despite its emergence as the new industry leader, there’s room in the growing space economy for other companies.

sum: Lockheed Martin (NYSE:LMT | LMT Price Prediction) dominates financial media, riding a record backlog and climbing stock price. Every defense analyst touts it. Lockheed’s story is real, but it’s priced in. The stock has climbed 24.21% over the past year…

Rheinmetall (OTC:RNMBY) sits quietly in the OTC market, largely ignored. It’s up just 1.84% over the past year and down 7.91% year to date. For a company that returned 1,661% over five years, this pause typically precedes another leg up.

At the 2025 NATO Summit in The Hague, allies committed to raising defense investment to 5% of GDP annually by 2035, up from the old 2% target most members were already struggling to meet. That is a decade-long procurement mandate. Rheinmetall, as Germany’s premier land systems and ammunition manufacturer, sits directly in that spending wave. European defense expenditure reached an estimated 2.1% of EU member states’ GDP in 2025, up from 1.6% in 2023. The runway to 5% is long and orders are flowing.

Europe is seeking significantly more autonomy, especially as the U.S. is showing signs that it might wind down support for Ukraine against Russia, leaving that up to Europe. For Europe to arm Ukraine by itself, it needs to massively invest in its manufacturing, which it has been doing so since 2022 and making good progress. And furthermore, Europe is also going beyond just rearming Ukraine and rearming itself to make sure other countries in Eastern Europe can be defended without tentative support from the U.S.

Rheinmetall reported full-year 2025 revenue of 9.94 billion euros, up 29% year over year, with an operating result of 1.84 billion euros, up 33%. The order backlog reached a record 63.8 billion euros, a 36% jump from the prior year. For 2026, the company guided for sales of 14 billion to 14.5 billion euros, representing growth of 40% to 45%, with an operating margin target of approximately 19%. The company expects its order backlog to more than double to 135 billion euros by year end. Lockheed’s record backlog of $194 billion gets celebrated in every earnings recap. Rheinmetall’s backlog is growing faster from a smaller base, with a cleaner balance sheet and no fixed-price contract exposure on classified programs.

items.t: Lockheed Martin stock surges despite earnings miss
sum: The company reported record deliveries of its F-35 fighter jet and a 9.1% increase in sales, but investors are looking further out

The aerospace and defense company reported earnings of $5.80 per share in the fourth quarter, which was slightly below the $5.85 analysts were expecting. Investors shrugged off the miss, though, and opted to focus on the company's 2026 outlook and other future business.
Shares of Lockheed Martin spiked more than 5% in pre-market trading Thursday.

The company's 2026 outlook is projecting net sales of $77.5 billion to $80 billion, which is in range (and perhaps slightly above) consensus estimates of $77.9 billion. In a separate release, however, Lockheed announced an agreement with the Department of Defense to "quadruple the production of Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) interceptors, from 96 to 400 interceptors per year.”
Terms of that deal were not announced, but Lockheed said it would spend billions of dollars over the next three years to expand production and modernize over 20 facilities.

THADD interceptors weren't the only source of good news. Lockheed said it saw record deliveries of its stealth F-35 fighter jets in the fourth quarter, which led to a 9.1% increase in sales. And investors seem encouraged after Donald Trump said the defense budget for fiscal 2027 could reach as high as $1.5 trillion.

Lockheed's earnings follow a quarterly sales jump of 57% at Boeing $BA, reported earlier this week. That airline manufacturer brought in $23.9 billion in the final quarter of 2025, a 57% increase over the same period in 2024 and delivered 600 airplanes last year, compared to 348 a year earlier.

sum: President Donald Trump on Wednesday said he "will not permit" defense companies to issue dividends or stock buybacks until those firms speed up their production of military equipment and address his other complaints about the industry.
Trump, in a lengthy Truth Social post, also took aim at defense contractors' executive pay packages, calling them "exorbitant and unjustifiable."
"Defense Companies are not producing our Great Military Equipment rapidly enough and, once produced, not maintaining it properly or quickly," he wrote.
Until those companies build new production plants, "no Executive should be allowed to make in excess of $5 Million Dollars," Trump declared.
Shares of General Dynamics, Lockheed Martin and Northrop Grumman each fell about 3% following Trump's comments.

Trump later singled out Raytheon as "the least responsive to the needs of the Department of War, the slowest in increasing their volume, and the most aggressive spending on their Shareholders rather than the needs and demands of the United States Military."

He said that the Pentagon will cut its business ties with Raytheon unless it "steps up" on investment in plants and equipment, adding that "under no circumstances" can the company do any more stock buybacks in the meantime.

items.t: There’s a ‘once-in-a-generation opportunity’ in these stocks, no matter how the AI boom ends
sum: Wall Street has overlooked a class of stocks that typically outperforms the market but is currently offering the best bargain in nearly 30 years, according to Ruchir Sharma, chair of Rockefeller International.

In a Financial Times column on Sunday, the market veteran said investors have thrown up their hands amid the ongoing debate about whether the AI boom is a bubble about to burst, while other assets look too pricey as well.

“But there is a once-in-a-generation opportunity in global markets that could deliver strong returns regardless of how AI mania plays out,” he wrote. “The opportunity is in quality stocks, particularly those trading at relatively inexpensive prices.”
Those stocks—which have high returns on equity, stable earnings growth, and low debt—have historically traded at high valuations, but not right now, Sharma said.
They are currently 10 percentage points behind the broader market in developed economies and trailing by 17 points in emerging economies.
“Typically, quality stocks have delivered their best returns after similar (but rare) periods of underperformance, which is why this moment feels so ripe,” he added.

While the Magnificent Seven group of stocks has emerged as a symbol of the AI boom, some of them actually fall into the quality category, such as hyperscalers Alphabet and Microsoft, according to Sharma.
